title: Das Hausgesinde
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 140. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 140 is not a story so much as a cumulative nonsense rhyme in Low German, built the way "The House That Jack Built" is: two travelers heading to Walpe fall into question and answer, naming a husband called Cham, a child called Grind, a cradle called Hippodeige, a servant called Machmirsrecht, each new link recapping every one before it. The pleasure is entirely in the accumulating chant and its absurd rhymes, which grow more unwieldy with each repetition.

sentences.l: “Where do you want [to go] to?” “To Walpe.”
sentences.n: The whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), and this is the whole of it: two women meet on the road, and each answer is added to the front of a growing refrain until the breath runs out. wust = willst; henne = hin, ‘thither’ — the verb of motion is left out, as German leaves it out in “wo willst du hin?”, so the literal line supplies [to go] in square brackets; Nah is nach, ‘to,’ not nah, ‘near.’ Walpe is a village name, chosen as much for its sound as for any place. The title, Das Hausgesinde, means the household — husband, child, cradle, farmhand, named here in that order.

sentences.t: „Ick nah Walpe, du nah Walpe; sam, sam, goh wie dann.“
sentences.l: “I to Walpe, you to Walpe; together, together, go we then.”
sentences.i: “I to Walpe, you to Walpe — come along, come along, let us go then.”
sentences.n: The refrain, and the verbs are all left out: ick nah Walpe = ich [gehe] nach Walpe. sam is zusammen, ‘together,’ used almost as a call — come along; goh wie dann = gehen wir dann, and this wie is wir, ‘we,’ not wie, ‘how.’ The wie of the questions that follow is the ordinary ‘how’ — the same three letters doing two jobs a line apart.

sentences.t: „Häst du auck ’n Mann? wie hedd din Mann?“ „Cham.“
sentences.l: “Have you also a husband? how is your husband called?” “Cham.”
sentences.i: “Have you a husband too? what is your husband’s name?” “Cham.”
sentences.n: Häst = hast; auck = auch; ’n = ein (not ihn); hedd = heißt; din = dein. Mann here is a husband. Every name in this tale rhymes with the thing it belongs to — Mann and Cham — and that is most of what the names are for. What Cham might mean beyond the rhyme is not clear; it is not a German word.

sentences.t: „Min Mann Cham, din Mann Cham: ick nah Walpe, du nah Walpe; sam, sam, goh wie dann.“
sentences.l: “My husband Cham, your husband Cham: I to Walpe, you to Walpe; together, together, go we then.”
sentences.i: “My husband Cham, your husband Cham — I to Walpe, you to Walpe, come along, come along, let us go then.”
sentences.n: min = mein, din = dein. The husband is set in front of the road-refrain, and every answer after this is added the same way, so the chain grows from the top.

sentences.t: „Häst du auck ’n Kind? wie hedd din Kind?“ „Grind.“
sentences.l: “Have you also a child? how is your child called?” “Grind.”
sentences.i: “Have you a child too? what is your child’s name?” “Grind.”
sentences.n: Grind is a real German word — a scab, a scurf on the head — and a repellent thing to call a child; it also rhymes with Kind, which is the point. In Low German grinen means to cry, which would suit a child too, so the name may be half a joke either way; the tale does not say.

sentences.t: „Min Kind Grind, din Kind Grind: min Mann Cham, din Mann Cham: ick nah Walpe, du nah Walpe; sam, sam, goh wie dann.“
sentences.l: “My child Grind, your child Grind: my husband Cham, your husband Cham: I to Walpe, you to Walpe; together, together, go we then.”
sentences.i: “My child Grind, your child Grind — my husband Cham, your husband Cham — I to Walpe, you to Walpe, come along, come along, let us go then.”
sentences.n: The child now stands ahead of the husband; nothing else has changed. The refrain returns unchanged at the end of every exchange, with the newest answer set in front of it.

sentences.t: „Häst du auck ’n Weige? wie hedd dine Weige?“ „Hippodeige.“
sentences.l: “Have you also a cradle? how is your cradle called?” “Hippodeige.”
sentences.i: “Have you a cradle too? what is your cradle’s name?” “Hippodeige.”
sentences.n: Weige is Wiege, a cradle, and dine = deine. Hippodeige is invention: -deige gives the rhyme with Weige and may carry a hint of Teig, dough, but the front of it means nothing at all. Naming a cradle at all is part of the joke — the household is being counted, furniture and all.

sentences.t: „Mine Weige Hippodeige, dine Weige Hippodeige; min Kind Grind, din Kind Grind: min Mann Cham, din Mann Cham: ick nah Walpe, du nah Walpe; sam, sam, goh wie dann.“
sentences.l: “My cradle Hippodeige, your cradle Hippodeige; my child Grind, your child Grind: my husband Cham, your husband Cham: I to Walpe, you to Walpe; together, together, go we then.”
sentences.i: “My cradle Hippodeige, your cradle Hippodeige — my child Grind, your child Grind — my husband Cham, your husband Cham — I to Walpe, you to Walpe, come along, come along, let us go then.”
sentences.n: The cradle joins the chain ahead of the child; mine = meine, dine = deine.

sentences.t: „Häst du auck ’n Knecht? wie hedd din Knecht?“ „Machmirsrecht.“
sentences.l: “Have you also a farmhand? how is your farmhand called?” “Machmirsrecht.”
sentences.i: “Have you a farmhand too? what is your farmhand’s name?” “Machmirsrecht.”
sentences.n: Knecht is a farmhand or manservant, the last member of the Hausgesinde. Machmirsrecht is the one name that is transparent: mach mirs recht, “do it right for me, suit me” — a servant named for what is asked of him, and rhyming with Knecht into the bargain.

sentences.t: „Min Knecht Machmirsrecht, din Knecht Machmirsrecht: mine Weige Hippodeige, dine Weige Hippodeige: min Kind Grind, din Kind Grind: min Mann Cham, din Mann Cham: ick nah Walpe, du nah Walpe; sam, sam, goh wie dann.“
sentences.l: “My farmhand Machmirsrecht, your farmhand Machmirsrecht: my cradle Hippodeige, your cradle Hippodeige: my child Grind, your child Grind: my husband Cham, your husband Cham: I to Walpe, you to Walpe; together, together, go we then.”
sentences.i: “My farmhand Machmirsrecht, your farmhand Machmirsrecht — my cradle Hippodeige, your cradle Hippodeige — my child Grind, your child Grind — my husband Cham, your husband Cham — I to Walpe, you to Walpe, come along, come along, let us go then.”
sentences.n: The whole chain, and the end: farmhand, cradle, child, husband, road. Nothing is resolved because there is nothing to resolve — the accumulation is the tale, of the kind recited until the reciter runs out of breath.

glossary.grind: Grind — the child’s name; the German word means a scab or scurf, and it rhymes with Kind (Low German grinen, to cry, may also be heard in it)
glossary.n: Low German: ’n — ein, a (‘’n Mann’ = ein Mann)
glossary.nah: Low German: nach — to, toward (‘nah Walpe’ = nach Walpe)
glossary.wie: Low German: wir — we (‘goh wie dann’ = gehen wir dann); also wie — how (‘wie hedd din Mann?’ = wie heißt dein Mann?)
glossary.wust: wollen — will, want (2nd sg.; Low German = willst)
